title: The Scientific Revolution: When We Learned How to Learn
subtitle: For millennia, 'truth' meant what ancient authorities said. Then a new rule appeared: test it against reality. That rule changed everything.
hook: For most of history, the way to settle a question was to ask what Aristotle or scripture said. Then, over the 1500s–1600s, a radical idea took hold: don't trust authority — *test* it. Observe, measure, experiment, and let reality be the referee. That's the **scientific method**, and it wasn't a discovery so much as an upgrade to *how we discover*. Today: the invention that made every other modern invention possible.

sections.heading: From authority to evidence
sections.body: The revolution's core move was demoting **authority** and promoting **evidence**. Copernicus and Galileo said: don't ask what the ancients decreed the heavens do — *look* through the telescope. Bacon and others formalized it: form a hypothesis, run an experiment, measure, and update. Crucially, results had to be **repeatable** by others — truth became something anyone could check, not something you had to be told.

sections.caption: The upgrade: stop asking authority, start asking reality — hypothesize, test, measure, and update, with others able to repeat it.

sections.label: Why it compounds
sections.body: Science's superpower is that it's **cumulative and self-correcting**. Each verified result becomes a foundation others build on; each wrong idea eventually gets falsified and dropped. Unlike appeals to authority, it has a built-in error-correction mechanism — which is why knowledge started growing *exponentially* (yesterday's curve!) rather than drifting sideways for centuries.

sections.label: The press lit the fuse
sections.body: This didn't happen in a vacuum: the printing press (our last History lesson) let results, data, and challenges to orthodoxy circulate fast enough for a community of investigators to check and build on each other's work. Cheap copying + 'test it yourself' = a knowledge engine. The two inventions together are why the modern world accelerated.

sections.caption: The Scientific Revolution — how the method of testing ideas took hold.

takeaways: The revolution demoted **authority** and promoted **evidence** — ask reality, not the ancients.
The **scientific method**: hypothesize → experiment → measure → update.
Results had to be **repeatable** — truth anyone can check, not something decreed.
Science is **cumulative and self-correcting**, so knowledge began growing exponentially.
The **printing press** lit the fuse by letting a community verify and build on each other's work.

quiz.q: What was the core shift of the Scientific Revolution?
options: From trusting authority to testing ideas against evidence
quiz.explain: Reality, not authority, became the referee — the scientific method.

quiz.q: Why does science 'compound' where appeals to authority don't?
options: It's cumulative and self-correcting — verified results stack up, wrong ones get falsified
quiz.explain: Built-in error correction lets knowledge grow instead of drifting.

quiz.q: CALLBACK: How did the printing press (Day 8) enable this?
options: Cheap copies let results and challenges circulate fast, so a community could verify and build on each other's work
quiz.explain: Cheap copying + 'test it yourself' = a knowledge engine. The two inventions compound together.

tg_quiz.q: The Scientific Revolution's big move was…
tg_quiz.correct: Right — reality, not authority, became the referee.
tg_quiz.wrong: It flipped to testing ideas against evidence — the scientific method.
